name: Cochlea Barren
description: Cochlea Barren is a tiny, airless world whose surface features a single enormous spiral crater that coils inward from the southern hemisphere like the cochlea of an inner ear. The crater's spiral walls descend in smooth, even turns to a central depression of perfect circularity, a geometry too regular for a natural impact event. The rest of the surface is pocked and dusty, unremarkable in every way that the spiral is extraordinary.

The near-zero gravity means that any disturbance to the surface dust sends it drifting upward in slow-motion clouds that take hours to settle. The silence is absolute, and the spiral crater creates an optical illusion from its rim, appearing to descend infinitely as the eye follows the tightening coils inward. Solar wind has polished the spiral walls to a metallic sheen while leaving the surrounding terrain rough and dull.

A signal has been detected emanating from the exact center of the spiral, a transmission so faint it was only discovered by a probe that happened to pass within close range. The signal is not electromagnetic but gravitational, a ripple in spacetime detectable only by the most sensitive instruments. The spiral's geometry corresponds to no natural formation process, and core samples from its walls show material that was heated and compressed to a degree inconsistent with any known impact event.

Cochlea Barren's gravitational signal has attracted the attention of physicists studying exotic spacetime phenomena, who theorize the spiral may be an artifact of technology that operated on gravitational principles. The planet's small size and low gravity make landing easy, but the signal's effects on instruments grow unpredictable near the spiral's center. Several research proposals are competing for priority access, and the planet's status as a potential first-contact artifact has complicated what was expected to be a routine survey authorization.
